newsitem.title: ERITREA: Sudan rebels say they nearing strategic dam.
newsitem.headline: Sudan rebels say they nearing strategic dam.

text.p: Sudanese rebels said on Wednesday they seized two government army garrisons in eastern Sudan and were only some 30 km (19 miles) from strategic Roseires dam.
Yassir Arman, a spokesman for the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), said National Democratic Alliance forces captured the garrisons at Yarda and Darfa and were advancing towards Wad el-Mahal.
"They are now 30 km (19 miles) from Roseires and five km (three miles) from Kirma, which is an outpost 25 km (15 miles) from Roseires," he told Reuters in the Eritrean capital Asmara.
He quoted SPLA leader John Garang, the NDA's military chairman, that all the garrisons captured by the rebels since the start of their offensive on January 12 remained in their hands.

But Arman said the rebels were not primarily interested in capturing Damazin, separated from Roseires by a bridge over the Blue Nile. The hydroelectric plant there supplies Khartoum with 80 percent of its electricity.
"We are not primarily interested in capturing Damazin," he said. "We want to inflict a heavy damage on the NIF (National Islamic Front) military and security to enable an uprising."
There have been no independent accounts of the fighting since the NDA launched its offensive in the east and it is difficult to assess the veracity of reports by both sides.

A Western diplomat in Nairobi said he doubted the rebels could seize Damazin and Roseires because they were too important to the government and that there was no apparent chance the rebel offensive would unleash an uprising in the capital.
"The goal of this current offensive is clearly political pressure to get Khartoum either to collapse or at least to push it into some serious negotiations," the diplomat told Reuters.
"They want something this year...but Khartoum will try and buy time," he added. "The major obstacle for the rebels however is the presence of a recalcitrant or worse Hassan al-Turabi."
Turabi is Sudan's speaker of parliament and the Islamist idealogue behind the military-dominated government in Khartoum.

"At this point it looks like Turabi will tough it out...he genuinely believes he can ride this bucking bronco to a standstill but his losing his cool recently indicates he views it seriously," said the diplomat, who declined to be identified.
The SPLA earlier on Wednesday denied the government army had opened a new battlefront near the Sudanese border with Uganda.

An SPLA statement said Khartoum was "peddling lies" by saying its troops attacked a rebel base near the border with Uganda following fighting in eastern Sudan near the borders with Ethiopia and Eritrea.
"No fighting has taken place in that area since successful SPLA operations...last year," said the statement, adding the site of the attack as reported by Khartoum did not even exist.
"The claim by the NIF regime there was fighting on Sunday January 26, 1997, in the Blue Nile area where they allegedly killed 300 Ethiopian troops is equally untrue," the SPLA added.
Eritrea and Ethiopia both deny Khartoum's accusations that their troops are fighting alongside the rebels in the east.
